alt: For each edge Kruskal's algorithm accepts, one group of cities is marked as one side of a cut and every other city is the other side. The edges crossing that cut are highlighted, and the cheapest of them is the accepted edge.

steps.caption: The same 6 cities and 8 costed edges as before. A cut splits the cities into two sides; an edge crosses the cut when its ends are on different sides. Kruskal's algorithm accepts an edge only when it is the cheapest edge across some cut.
Cut: the group {3} on one side, every other city on the other. The edges across it are 3-4 (2), 2-3 (4), 0-3 (6), 3-5 (9). The cheapest, 3-4 at 2, is the edge Kruskal accepts, so it is safe.
Cut: the group {1} on one side, every other city on the other. The edges across it are 1-2 (3), 0-1 (5), 1-4 (7). The cheapest, 1-2 at 3, is the edge Kruskal accepts, so it is safe.
Cut: the group {1, 2} on one side, every other city on the other. The edges across it are 2-3 (4), 0-1 (5), 1-4 (7), 0-2 (8). The cheapest, 2-3 at 4, is the edge Kruskal accepts, so it is safe.
Cut: the group {0} on one side, every other city on the other. The edges across it are 0-1 (5), 0-3 (6), 0-2 (8). The cheapest, 0-1 at 5, is the edge Kruskal accepts, so it is safe.
Cut: the group {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} on one side, every other city on the other. The edges across it are 3-5 (9). The cheapest, 3-5 at 9, is the edge Kruskal accepts, so it is safe.
Every accepted edge was the cheapest across some cut, so together they form a minimum spanning tree of cost 23.
